disclaimer: These notes were written with AI assistance, drawing on standard commentaries. For study only.

dafengge.summary: A three-line song in the Chu-song style, improvised by Liu Bang after he put down a rebellion and went home to feast with his townsfolk. The great wind and flying clouds suggest his might, and 'my power spreads within the seas' is his triumph, but the last line turns to worry: where will he find brave men to guard the realm? Pride and anxiety sit side by side.
dafengge.translation:
A great wind rises, oh, and the clouds fly high.
My might spreads over all within the seas, oh, and I come home to my village.
Where shall I find brave warriors, oh, to guard the four quarters?

glossary.note: A particle that carries the sound of the line, rather like a long 'oh' or 'ah'. It is typical of the Chu ci (Songs of Chu) style, which this song imitates.
Everything within the four seas, that is, the whole world as the ancient Chinese pictured it. It means 'all under Heaven'.
To bring to bear on, or to extend over. Here his authority reaches everywhere.
Courageous and powerful fighting men, the generals and soldiers a ruler needs to hold his territory.

dafengge.background: By Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu of the Han), founder of the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD). Tradition says that after crushing the rebellion of Ying Bu, King of Huainan, he returned to his home county of Pei, drank with the village elders, and sang this song while beating a zhu, a stringed instrument struck with a bamboo stick.

gaixiage.summary: The last poem of Xiang Yu, the Hegemon-King of Western Chu, written when the Han army had him surrounded at Gaixia. The first two lines boast of a strength that could shake mountains; the last two admit that fortune has turned, even his horse will not go forward, and all he can do is sigh to his beloved Lady Yu. It is both grand and desolate.
gaixiage.translation:
My strength can pull up mountains, oh, my spirit towers over the age.
But the times are against me, oh, and my dappled horse will not run.
My dappled horse will not run, oh, what can be done?
Yu, oh Yu, oh Yu, what shall I do about you?

glossary.en: ba shan - 'to pull up a mountain'
glossary.note: Strong enough to uproot a mountain, a way of describing enormous strength.

glossary.en: qi gai shi - 'spirit that covers the age'
glossary.note: A spirit and bearing that surpass everyone of his time.
A horse with a grey-and-white mottled coat. Here it means Xiang Yu's famous mount, Wuzhui, the Black Dappled Horse.
To advance or run ahead. The horse will not move on.
Yu Ji, Xiang Yu's beloved consort, who stayed at his side through the campaigns. Tradition says she died by her own hand that night.
An old second-person pronoun. The last line addresses Lady Yu directly.

gaixiage.background: By Xiang Yu, as recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), 'Basic Annals of Xiang Yu'. Surrounded at Gaixia by the Han army, he heard Chu songs sung on every side in the night, which told him that Chu land had fallen, and he took leave of Lady Yu with this song.

shangye.summary: A folk song from the Han yuefu (Music Bureau) collection in which a woman swears to Heaven that she and her beloved will be bound together, and that she will break with him only when mountains flatten, rivers run dry, thunder rolls in winter, snow falls in summer, and sky and earth join. Five impossible things in a row give the vow its fierce heat.

glossary.note: A cry in which the speaker calls on Heaven as witness to her oath. The second character is an old variant of a particle, so the phrase simply means 'O Heaven!'.

glossary.en: xiang zhi - 'to be at one in feeling'
glossary.note: To love each other and understand each other's hearts, a deeper bond than merely knowing someone.
Here it works like 'to make something so'. 'Long may it last' means 'may our love be made to endure'.
A mountain peak or a big mound of earth. The oath imagines every one of them levelled.
To be exhausted or dried up, said of a river or spring.
Here the word for rain is used as a verb meaning 'to fall as snow', and it is read yu (fourth tone), not the usual noun reading.

shangye.background: A Han yuefu folk song, included among the 'Nao ge' (drum-and-cymbal) songs, a group of eighteen military and ceremonial pieces. The title is simply its opening words.

jiangnan.summary: A light Han yuefu folk song about lotus picking in the south. The lotus leaves are thick and bright, and fish play among them, and the poem repeats 'east, west, south, north' as if following the fish around the pond. The pace is quick, and the mood is carefree and full of everyday life.
jiangnan.translation:
In the south of the river one can gather lotus,
how thick and round the lotus leaves are!
Fish play among the lotus leaves.
Fish play to the east of the lotus leaves,
fish play to the west of the lotus leaves,
fish play to the south of the lotus leaves,
fish play to the north of the lotus leaves.

glossary.en: ke - 'can, it is the time for'
glossary.note: Suitable, or just right. The phrase says it is a good time to go and gather lotus.

glossary.en: he tian tian - 'how thick and round'
glossary.note: The reduplicated word describes lotus leaves spreading across the water like a layer of round pads, close together and lush.
To play about happily. The fish are in no hurry.
In the watery country south of the Yangtze, lotus gathering was both a job and an outing, usually done by girls in small boats, and it became a favourite subject of later poets.

jiangnan.background: A Han yuefu folk song, filed under the 'Xianghe ge ci' (songs sung to accompaniment) group of the Music Bureau collection.

changgexing.summary: A Han yuefu 'Long Song' that starts with sunflowers in a garden, bathed in dew and sunlight, to make a point about time. Everything flourishes and then fades, and rivers that run east do not return, so the poem closes with a plain warning: if you do not work hard while young and strong, you will only grieve when old.
changgexing.translation:
Green, green are the mallows in the garden;
the morning dew waits for the sun to dry it.
Spring spreads its kindness,
and all things shine with light.
I always fear the autumn season will come
and the flowers and leaves will turn yellow and fall.
A hundred rivers run east to the sea;
when will they ever flow back west?
If you do not strive while young and strong,
in old age you will grieve in vain.

glossary.note: The winter mallow, a leafy vegetable that was common on ancient Chinese tables and grew in many gardens.
To dry out, here by the morning sun. The dew waits for the sun that will dry it, which already hints at how short things last.
Spring is pictured as a giver of kindness, spreading warmth and rain over all living things.
The yellowing colour of leaves that are starting to wither in autumn.
Flowers and foliage together. The line fears the moment they all wither.

glossary.en: lao da tu shang bei - 'old, and grieving in vain'
glossary.note: When one has grown old, regret is useless. This is the moral of the whole poem, and the line has become a well-known proverb about using one's youth.

changgexing.background: A Han yuefu folk song, and one of the best-known poems urging people to treasure time.

shiwucongjun.summary: A narrative yuefu poem about an old soldier who went to the army at fifteen and came home only at eighty. He finds his house in ruins and his family's graves in rows. He gathers wild grain and greens and cooks a meal, but there is no one to share it with, and at last he goes out the door, looks east, and weeps. The poem protests against war and conscription.
shiwucongjun.translation:
At fifteen I went off to the army,
at eighty I was finally allowed home.
On the road I met a man from my village:
'Who is left in my house?'
'Over there, that is your house,
with pines and cypresses and grave mounds, row on row.'
Hares run in through the dog hole,
pheasants fly up from the rafters.
In the courtyard grows wild grain,
over the well grow wild mallows.
I pound the grain to make rice,
pick the mallows to make soup.
Soup and rice are ready at once,
but I do not know whom to give them to!
I go out the door and look east,
tears fall and wet my clothes.

glossary.note: A colloquial word for 'who'. The first syllable is only a prefix, as in 'A-mei' for a name.
A burial mound or tomb. The old man sees that his whole family has become graves.
A reduplicated word for things piled up or lined up one after another, here the grave mounds.
The small opening in a wall or gate through which a dog could go in and out. Wild hares now use it, a sign that the house is abandoned.
Grain that grows by itself, not planted by anyone. 'Lu' here means 'wild' or 'self-sown'.
A soup or stew with liquid in it, made here from the wild greens.

shiwucongjun.background: A Han yuefu folk song. It reflects the hardship that long military service brought to ordinary people in the Han period.

chilege.summary: A folk song from the Northern Dynasties (386-581) that paints the great grassland of the Chile plain: the Yin Mountains behind it, a sky like a huge tent over the fields, and a wind that bends the grass to show herds of cattle and sheep. The words are plain, the scene is vast, and the feeling is of open steppe.
chilege.translation:
The Chile plain,
beneath the Yin Mountains.
The sky is like a felt tent,
covering the fields on every side.
The sky is deep blue, the plain stretches without end;
the wind blows, the grass bends low, and cattle and sheep appear.

glossary.note: The flat land where the Chile people lived. The Chile were a nomadic people of the northern steppes, and 'chuan' means a broad river plain.
The Yin Mountain range, in what is now Inner Mongolia, running along the northern edge of the Yellow River bend.
A round-topped tent of felt, the kind of dwelling known today as a yurt or Mongolian ger. The sky is likened to one.
Here the character is used for the one meaning 'to show itself' or 'to come into view'. The cattle and sheep are revealed when the grass bends.
A reduplicated word for a deep, far-reaching blue-green, here the colour of the open sky.

chilege.background: A folk song of the Northern Dynasties. Tradition says it was first sung in the Xianbei language and later turned into Chinese.

mulanci.summary: A long narrative poem of the Northern Dynasties (386-581) about Mulan, who takes her father's place in the army disguised as a man. After twelve years she returns in triumph, refuses office, goes home, puts on women's clothes again, and astonishes her comrades. The pace is brisk and the repetitions are lively, and the ending, with its image of the male and female hare, is witty and strong.
mulanci.translation:
Click, click, and click again,
Mulan sits weaving at the door.
You cannot hear the sound of the loom,
only the girl's sighs.
We ask the girl what is on her mind,
we ask the girl what she is thinking of.
'The girl has nothing on her mind,
the girl is thinking of nothing.
Last night I saw the army notice:
the Khan is calling up troops on a grand scale.
The army lists run to twelve scrolls,
and in every scroll is my father's name.
Father has no grown son,
Mulan has no elder brother.
I will buy a saddle and a horse,
and from now on go to war in Father's place.'
In the east market she buys a fine horse,
in the west market a saddle and blanket,
in the south market a bridle,
in the north market a long whip.
At dawn she says goodbye to Father and Mother,
at dusk she sleeps by the Yellow River.
She does not hear Father and Mother calling their daughter,
she hears only the Yellow River's water splashing and rushing.
At daybreak she leaves the Yellow River,
at dusk she reaches the top of Black Mountain.
She does not hear Father and Mother calling their daughter,
she hears only the neighing of barbarian cavalry on Mount Yan.
Ten thousand li she rushes to the war,
crossing passes and mountains as if on wings.
The northern cold carries the sound of the watchman's clapper,
and the chill light shines on iron armour.
Generals die in a hundred battles,
and brave men come home after ten years.
She comes back to see the Son of Heaven,
the Son of Heaven sits in the Hall of Light.
Her merit is recorded at twelve grades,
the rewards run to more than a hundred thousand.
The Khan asks what she wants.
'Mulan has no use for a post as Secretary of the Board.
I would only ask for a camel that can go a thousand li,
to take your servant home.'
When Father and Mother hear their daughter is coming,
they go out past the town wall to meet her, helping each other along.
When her elder sister hears her younger sister is coming,
she fixes her rouge and powder at the door.
When her little brother hears his sister is coming,
he sharpens his knife, whoosh, whoosh, for the pigs and sheep.
'Open the door of my east chamber,
let me sit on the bed in my west chamber.
I take off the robe I wore in war,
I put on the clothes I used to wear.'
At the window she arranges her cloud-like hair,
before the mirror she sticks on her yellow forehead mark.
She goes out to see her comrades,
and her comrades are all amazed and flustered:
'We marched together for twelve years
and never knew Mulan was a girl!'
The male hare kicks and scrabbles,
the female hare's eyes are blurred and dim.
But when two hares run side by side along the ground,
how can anyone tell which of us is male or female?

keyLines.note: The opening sound. Commentators disagree whether it is the sound of sighing or of the loom, but either way it leads straight into the picture of Mulan weaving at the door.

keyLines.line: 願為市鞍馬，從此替爺征
keyLines.en: I will buy a saddle and a horse, and from now on go to war in Father's place
keyLines.note: This is Mulan's decision to take her father's place in the army, and the turning point of the whole poem.

keyLines.line: 不聞爺孃喚女聲，但聞黃河流水鳴濺濺
keyLines.en: She does not hear Father and Mother calling their daughter, she hears only the Yellow River's water splashing and rushing
keyLines.note: The sound of the river stands in for the sound of her parents' voices. Her homesickness is felt through what she cannot hear, without being stated.

keyLines.line: 將軍百戰死，壯士十年歸
keyLines.en: Generals die in a hundred battles, and brave men come home after ten years
keyLines.note: In a few words, the line sums up ten years of hard fighting and how few survive it, which is more telling than a long account of battles.

keyLines.en: Mulan has no use for a post as Secretary of the Board
keyLines.note: Mulan does not want rank or office. She wants only to go home to her family.

keyLines.line: 雄兔腳撲朔，雌兔眼迷離
keyLines.en: The male hare kicks and scrabbles, the female hare's eyes are blurred and dim
keyLines.note: The closing comparison suggests that once the two hares are running, no one can tell them apart, and so a woman can win honour in war as well as any man.

glossary.note: The title northern peoples used for their ruler, here the sovereign of the Northern Dynasties.
An old colloquial word for father. 'Ye niang' means 'father and mother', that is, parents.
A wooden clapper struck to mark the night watches in a camp.

glossary.en: ce xun shi er zhuan - 'merit recorded at twelve grades'
glossary.note: The court recorded her deeds and promoted her. 'Zhuan' is a step up in the system of military honours, and twelve is the highest number of grades.
A yellow ornament that women of the time stuck on the forehead as make-up.
Soldiers who served in the same squad. In the army of the time ten men made a 'huo', a cooking group, so these are comrades who ate together.

mulanci.background: A folk song of the Northern Dynasties. The version we have was polished by later hands, and scholars differ on its date and on how it reached its final form.

duangexing.summary: A four-character yuefu poem by Cao Cao. It begins by lamenting how short life is, with wine and song to ease the worry, but its real theme is a thirst for talented men. It borrows lines from the Book of Songs (Shijing), and it ends with the Duke of Zhou, who gave up his meal to receive worthy visitors, to show Cao Cao's wish to treat gifted people with respect so that the whole world will turn to him.
duangexing.translation:
Facing wine, one should sing: how long is a human life?
It is like the morning dew, and the days gone by are very many.
The song is stirring and passionate, yet the sorrow is hard to forget.
What can dissolve this sorrow? Only Du Kang, wine.
The green collar of the scholar, how long my heart yearns for you.
Only because of you I have been murmuring this song until now.
The deer call 'you, you' to each other, eating the wild artemisia in the fields.
I have honoured guests, and for them we play the zither and blow the reed pipes.
Bright as the moon, when can it be plucked?
Sorrow wells up from within and cannot be cut off.
You crossed the paths between the fields, honouring me with a visit.
After long parting we talk and feast, and my heart remembers old kindness.
The moon is bright, the stars are few, and magpies fly south.
They circle the tree three times: on which branch can they rest?
The mountain does not tire of height, the sea does not tire of depth.
The Duke of Zhou spat out his food, and the world turned its heart to him.

keyLines.en: Facing wine, one should sing: how long is a human life?
keyLines.note: The opening line sighs over how short human life is.

keyLines.en: What can dissolve this sorrow? Only Du Kang, wine.
keyLines.note: Du Kang is said to be the first maker of wine, and his name is used here as another word for wine.

keyLines.en: The green collar of the scholar, how long my heart yearns for you.
keyLines.note: Taken from 'Zi jin' in the Book of Songs, in the section called Zheng Airs. It expresses longing for able men.

keyLines.en: The deer call 'you, you' to each other, eating the wild artemisia in the fields.
keyLines.note: Taken from 'Lu ming' (The Deer Cry) in the Lesser Odes of the Book of Songs. A feast for guests stands for the courtesy shown to the worthy.

keyLines.en: The moon is bright, the stars are few, and magpies fly south.
keyLines.note: The magpies wander with no place to perch, a picture of talented men who must choose a ruler worth settling with.

keyLines.en: The Duke of Zhou spat out his food, and the world turned its heart to him.
keyLines.note: By recalling the story of the Duke of Zhou, who rushed to receive worthy men, Cao Cao shows how he means to treat them.

glossary.note: It means 'should', and some also take it as 'facing' (wine).
He is said to have been the first to brew wine. Later his name became a word for wine itself.
Originally the blue-green collar of a robe. Here it stands for a scholar, or a man of talent.
A plant of the mugwort family, the wild herb the deer feed on in the song.

glossary.en: qi kuo tan yan - 'long parted, then talking and feasting'
glossary.note: Meeting again after a long separation and chatting over a banquet. The last character is an old form of the word for 'feast'.
The Duke of Zhou is said to have spat out a mouthful of food, more than once in a single meal, to receive visiting scholars at once.

duangexing.background: By Cao Cao (155-220), a statesman and poet at the end of the Han dynasty, and one of the best-known poems of the Jian'an era (196-220). Scholars differ on exactly when it was written.

guancanghai.summary: The first stanza of Cao Cao's 'Bu chu Xiamen xing' (Walking out of the Xia Gate). He climbs Jieshi Mountain and looks out over the sea: the water ripples, islands stand up out of it, the autumn wind is bleak, and great waves rise. He imagines the sun, moon and stars all coming out of the sea. The mood is expansive and the scene is mighty.
guancanghai.translation:
Going east I come to Jieshi,
and from it I look at the grey-blue sea.
How the water ripples and sways,
the mountain islands stand tall and sharp.
Trees and bushes grow in clumps,
and a hundred grasses are rich and lush.
The autumn wind blows bleak and chill,
and great waves surge up.
The course of the sun and the moon
seems to start from within it;
the glittering Milky Way
seems to come out from inside it.
How fortunate, how very fortunate,
we sing in order to voice our aims.

glossary.note: A hill by the sea in what is now the Changli area of Hebei province, a landmark for travellers on the coast.
The sea, whose waters look a deep blue-green. It is the usual poetic word for the ocean.
A reduplicated word for water moving in a gentle swaying way.
To rise up high and stand firm, said of the islands.
The river of stars, that is, the Milky Way.

glossary.en: xing shen zhi zai, ge yi yong zhi - 'how fortunate; we sing to voice our aims'
glossary.note: A set formula in yuefu poems, used to close a movement of a song. It does not describe the sea, and it has been used as a closing line in many such pieces.

guancanghai.background: By Cao Cao. It is thought to have been written about 207, when he was returning from a victorious northern campaign against the Wuhuan and passed Jieshi Mountain.

qibushi.summary: A short five-character poem built on one image: beans are boiled over a fire of their own stalks, and the beans weep in the pot. Beans and stalks grew from one root, so why should one press so hard on the other? It is a picture of brothers who destroy each other, put in simple words that move the reader.
qibushi.translation:
Boil the beans and burn the bean stalks,
the beans in the pot are weeping.
We were born from the same root,
why be so quick to scorch me?

glossary.note: The stems of bean plants, which when dried were used as firewood.
An old kind of cooking pot, a round-bellied vessel used to boil food.
To cry quietly or in a low voice, rather than wailing.

glossary.en: tong gen sheng - 'born of one root'
glossary.note: Grown from the same root. It stands for brothers of the same parents.
Literally to boil or fry something down; here it means to scorch, torment or press hard.

qibushi.background: By Cao Zhi (192-232), a son of Cao Cao and one of the finest poets of his age. According to the Shishuo xinyu (A New Account of Tales of the World), his brother Cao Pi, the Emperor Wen of Wei, told him to make a poem within seven steps or be put to death, and he made this one at once. The wording and even the authenticity of the poem have been disputed since early times.

yinjiu5.summary: The fifth of twenty poems called 'Drinking Wine'. It describes the mind of a recluse: he lives among people yet is not troubled by the noise of carriages, because his heart is far away. He picks chrysanthemums, looks up and sees the southern hills, and in the evening mist and the birds going home he senses the true meaning of nature, which words cannot fully say.
yinjiu5.translation:
I built my hut in the world of men,
yet I hear no noise of carriages and horses.
You ask me how this can be?
When the heart is far away, the place becomes remote of itself.
I pick chrysanthemums under the eastern fence,
and at leisure my eyes fall on the southern hills.
The mountain air is lovely at dusk,
and the birds fly home together.
In this there is a true meaning;
I want to explain it, but I have already forgotten the words.

glossary.note: To put up a simple dwelling. Tao uses it for his plain home.
The world of people, where others live, as against the wilderness.

glossary.en: you ran jian nan shan - 'at leisure, I see the southern hills'
glossary.note: One text reads 'look towards' the hills instead of 'see' them. Critics through the centuries have preferred 'see', which suggests that the hills simply came into view without being sought.
Usually taken to mean Mount Lu, near Tao's home. Some think it means any hills to the south.
The evening, when the day is turning to night.
The real sense or taste of life and nature, felt directly rather than argued.

yinjiu5.background: By Tao Yuanming (365-427), who left official life and went to live in the country. It is one of his best-known poems from that period.

yuantian1.summary: The first of five poems called 'Returning to My Fields and Gardens'. Tao Yuanming describes his decision to leave office and the joy that followed. From youth he disliked worldly ways, and he strayed into the 'dusty net' of officialdom for thirty years, like a caged bird or a fish in a pond that longs for its old forest and deep pool. Now, in a thatched house with elms, willows, chickens and dogs and smoke over the village, he has at last returned to nature.
yuantian1.translation:
From youth I had no taste for the ways of the world,
by nature I loved the hills and mountains.
By mistake I fell into the dusty net,
and once gone, thirty years went by.
The caged bird longs for its old woods,
the fish in the pond thinks of its former deep pool.
I open up wasteland at the edge of the southern fields,
and holding to my simple nature, I return to field and garden.
My plot is ten mu or so,
my thatched house has eight or nine rooms.
Elms and willows shade the back eaves,
peach and plum trees are set out before the hall.
Dim and far off lies a village,
softly the smoke from the hamlets drifts up.
A dog barks in a deep lane,
a cock crows from the top of a mulberry tree.
My house and yard are free of dust and noise,
in the bare rooms there is leisure to spare.
For so long I was inside the cage;
now I can go back to what is natural.

glossary.en: shi su yun - 'a nature suited to the world'
glossary.note: A temperament that fits in with worldly ways and conventions. Tao says he never had one.
A figure for the bonds of officialdom and worldly life, a net made of dust and cares in which one is caught.
This is the reading of the common text, though some editions read 'thirteen years'. Tao in fact served only on and off over some thirteen years, so the point is debated.
To keep to one's plain, unpolished nature and not follow the crowd. 'Zhuo' means clumsy, which Tao takes as a quality.
A reduplicated word for something dim or faint, as a village looks in the distance in evening haze.
A cage for keeping birds and animals, again a figure for the confinement of an official career.

yuantian1.background: By Tao Yuanming. It is thought to have been written about 405, after he resigned as magistrate of Pengze and went back to farm.
